lesson.menu_desc: Giving bad news -- de-escalation and reframing with cleft sentences -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- The Client Who Is Wrong
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 15 -- The Client Who Is Wrong
lesson.grammar_point: cleft sentences for focus and reframing (what... is, it is... that)

listenings.text: I have been a doctor for twenty-two years, and I still remember the first time I gave a patient bad news. I said it all in one breath, in the corridor, and then I kept talking because the silence frightened me. Nobody heard a word after the first sentence. What I do now is very different. I sit down, so that we are at the same level. I give a warning first, something like: I'm afraid the results are not what we hoped. Then I stop, and I let the silence do its work. It is the silence that gives people time to understand, not my explanation. When they are ready, they ask the next question, and that tells me how much they want to know. And I never sugarcoat it. People can forgive bad news. What they never forget is the feeling that somebody was not honest with them.

I ran the complaints team for an airline for nine years, so I have been shouted at in four languages. The first thing I teach new staff is what not to say. Never say calm down. Nobody in the history of the world has calmed down because somebody told them to. Let the customer vent. Most people run out of anger in about ninety seconds if you do not interrupt. Then name the feeling: I can see this has ruined your trip. Only after that do you move to the facts. And when the facts are bad, change the frame. Do not say: there is nothing we can do. Say: what we can do today is this. The situation is the same, but the conversation is now about the next step, not about the last mistake. That is what defuses it. You are not hiding the bad news. You are giving the person somewhere to go.
